meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The real tragedy of the poor is the poverty of their aspirations'?
meta.ogDescription: Adam Smith never wrote it — the line is absent from his works. The usual fix, Ernest Bevin, has no primary source either. Origin unknown.

answer.label: Not Adam Smith — usually credited to Ernest Bevin
answer.authorDates: 1881–1951 · British trade union leader, Minister of Labour & Foreign Secretary
answer.sourceLine: Adam Smith did not write this. The word ‘aspiration’ does not occur anywhere in The Wealth of Nations or The Theory of Moral Sentiments, and the Adam Smith Institute states flatly that he never said it. The line is usually re-credited to the Labour politician Ernest Bevin — but that attribution is itself undocumented: no speech, book, or dated source has been located, and Bevin’s own Wikiquote page does not list it.

source.excerpt: The real tragedy of the poor is the poverty of their aspirations.
trail: The simplest test first: search Smith’s own books. The word ‘aspiration’ does not appear a single time in the complete text of The Wealth of Nations ↗, nor in The Essays of Adam Smith ↗, the volume carrying The Theory of Moral Sentiments. Neither book contains the phrase ‘tragedy of the poor’.

Smith’s own institute says the same thing in plainer words. Sam Bowman, writing for the Adam Smith Institute ↗, states that Smith “never said” it, “as some people who have never read him think”, and that it is hard to think of a less Smithian view — Smith having had deep compassion for people unlucky in life.

The trail then points at Ernest Bevin, and stops. The LSE’s British Politics and Policy blog ↗ records only that New Labour in the 2000s “rediscovered the expression ‘poverty of aspiration’ – whose origin has been attributed to Labour politician Ernest Bevin”. Attributed by whom, when, and where is not said.

And the Bevin credit does not survive checking either: the line is missing from Bevin’s sourced Wikiquote page ↗ and from his Wikipedia biography, while the quote site that assigns it to him ↗ supplies no speech, book, or date. Quote Investigator has not examined this quote at all.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller passage to show, because no passage has ever been found. This is the line exactly as it circulates — free-floating, sourceless, and attached to whichever famous name is nearest.

sourceLink.text: Adam Smith Institute: “Adam Smith never said that”

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted, because no source work has been identified. The line is not from Adam Smith, so his pre-1931 public-domain works do not cover it; and if it does trace to Ernest Bevin (d. 1951) or to some unidentified twentieth-century writer, the containing work could well still be in copyright. Treat the wording as of unknown origin and unknown status rather than assuming it is free to reuse.

author.name: Ernest Bevin
author.kicker: The name the correction points to
author.heading: So who was Ernest Bevin?
author.metaLine: 1881–1951 · British trade unionist, wartime Minister of Labour & post-war Foreign Secretary
author.bio: The seventh child of Diana Bevin — a Somerset domestic servant and village midwife who called herself a widow after her husband walked out four years before Ernest was born — Bevin never knew who his father was. He left school at eleven, drove a lorry in Bristol, and built the Transport and General Workers’ Union into Britain’s most powerful labour organisation, serving as its General Secretary from 1922. Churchill made him Minister of Labour in 1940; Attlee made him Foreign Secretary in 1945. He is the figure most often named as the origin of the phrase ‘poverty of aspiration’ — a coinage New Labour revived in the 2000s — though no primary source for these exact words has ever been produced, and the credit may be as loose as the Adam Smith one it was meant to correct.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located in the works of Adam Smith or Ernest Bevin. Clearest rebuttal consulted: Sam Bowman, “Ideas can mean the difference between wealth and poverty,” Adam Smith Institute blog, adamsmith.org (accessed 15 July 2026), which states that Smith never said it. On the Bevin credit, see Konstanze Spohrer, “The problem with ‘raising aspiration’ strategies,” LSE British Politics and Policy, 9 May 2018.

misattribution.heading: The attribution chain, link by link
misattribution.intro: This is a quote with two attributions and zero sources. One is demonstrably wrong; the other is merely unproven.

items.why: BrainyQuote, QuoteFancy, Quotation.io and dozens of aggregators run it under Smith’s name with no citation. His own institute disagrees: the Adam Smith Institute ↗ says he “never said” it and that it is hard to think of a less Smithian view. The full texts of The Wealth of Nations ↗ and The Essays of Adam Smith ↗ contain the word ‘aspiration’ not once.

The standard fix online. There is a real association between Bevin and the phrase ‘poverty of aspiration’ — the LSE ↗ notes New Labour revived the expression in the 2000s and that its origin “has been attributed to” him. But that is a passive credit for a phrase, not a citation for this sentence, and Bevin’s sourced Wikiquote page ↗ does not carry the line at all.

items.who: BrainyQuote, QuoteFancy, allgreatquotes and the rest
items.why: QuoteFancy ↗ is typical: Smith’s name, a wallpaper-ready layout, and no book, no year, no page. Even the site that gets the author ‘right’ — Lib Quotes ↗, which credits Bevin and flags the Smith error — offers no citation of its own.
The error travels: an Australian opinion piece ↗ built an entire article around the line, opening with the claim that it “is from Adam Smith” — and was corrected in its own comments.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody has produced a source for these words — not for Smith, not for Bevin. The honest answer is that the origin is unknown, and the one thing we can say with confidence ↗ is that it is not Adam Smith’s.

context.heading: Why this one keeps landing on Adam Smith
lead: The quote has the shape of an economist’s aphorism — a crisp inversion, a diagnosis of poverty that locates the problem inside the poor rather than around them. Adam Smith is the default signature for anything that sounds like economics and reads like a maxim, which is exactly how a line with no traceable origin ends up under the most famous name in the field.

The irony is that the sentiment cuts against Smith. He wrote that no society can be flourishing and happy where the greater part of its members are poor and miserable, and his account of poverty is structural, not a scolding of the poor for wanting too little. The Adam Smith Institute — hardly a hostile witness — calls the line the opposite of Smith’s voice and puts it down to people who have never read him.
context.detailsSummary: The Bevin correction — and why it isn’t the end of the story
detailsBody: The usual fix, repeated on quote sites and in comment threads, is that the real author is Ernest Bevin. There is a genuine thread here: the phrase ‘poverty of aspiration’ does have a Bevin association in British political memory, and New Labour revived the expression in the 2000s to explain educational outcomes among working-class children.

But an association is not a citation. The LSE’s own account says only that the phrase’s origin has been attributed to Bevin — passive, unsourced, and about the phrase rather than this sentence. No Hansard record, speech text, or biography has been produced for these words, and Bevin’s Wikiquote page does not include them. Correcting a fake Smith quote with an undocumented Bevin quote just moves the problem.
context.pull: It is hard to think of a less Smithian view.
